opening.headline: We examine why attempting to handle complex tasks with a single prompt fails, and learn three fundamental patterns for breaking down work: chaining, routing, and parallelization.
body: Translating, standardizing terminology, adjusting tone, and checking for errors all requested within a single prompt often fails to adequately address any one of these tasks. When a single call handles multiple considerations, attention is inevitably distributed across them, leading to reduced focus on each individual aspect.

In this lesson, we will sequentially examine prompt chaining for dividing tasks, routing inputs by team, and parallelization for processing multiple tasks simultaneously. Finally, we will design and compare workflows for document translation and quality review using chaining and parallel voting, and establish criteria for selecting appropriate patterns based on task characteristics.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain prompt chaining, routing, and parallelization.
You can distinguish patterns that fit your work characteristics.

items.prompt: What did you ask for in one go in the prompt?
items.answer: We have included all four requirements—translation, terminology standardization, tone alignment, and error verification—within a single prompt. It's easy for people to miss one or more of these when asked to perform them all at once.

The terminology is correct, but the tone is inconsistent, and some of the review items are missing. This is not an error; it is a result of the model failing to balance handling of the entire requirement.

According to Anthropic's explanation, complex tasks involving multiple considerations are generally performed more effectively when each consideration is handled separately through a distinct call. This is because each call can focus on a specific aspect.

items.prompt: What happens when input types are diverse?
items.answer: Adjusting prompts to match one type of input may result in poor performance on other types of input. Attempting to optimize a single prompt for all inputs will ultimately lead to mutual inefficiencies.

items.prompt: What is the starting point of this course?
items.answer: Dividing work makes each call a simpler task. Depending on how it is divided, it can be sequentially chained, routed into branches, or parallelized to handle multiple tasks simultaneously.

screens.outro: Let me think about whether you have had a similar experience.

screens.title: Recall the experience of handling work in stages.
screens.lead: After first thinking through the question mentally and making a choice, the instructor's thought process is revealed. Answers are not entered or submitted.

items.prompt: Have you ever handled work in a step-by-step manner?
items.answer: A typical approach is to divide the report into an outline, draft, and revision. This division makes each stage a simpler task, and each subsequent stage builds upon the results of the previous one. The following screen demonstrates the concept of prompt chaining.

items.prompt: Was there a point where results could be verified between stages?
items.answer: If, before drafting the initial version, you verify that the outline meets the requirements, then that is your gate. Without an intermediate check, a flawed outline will persist all the way to the end, and the problem will only surface at the final stage.

items.prompt: Have you ever reviewed the same input simultaneously with multiple people?
items.answer: In some cases, the contract is reviewed simultaneously by legal, financial, and security personnel. They do not wait for each other's feedback, enabling a quick review process that stops immediately if any one person identifies an issue. This structure is analogous to a voting mechanism in parallel processing.

screens.outro: Let's view this experience through three patterns. First, prompt chaining.

screens.title: Prompt Chaining and Gates
screens.lead: This is an example of translating a product introduction, where you can follow step by step how the chain progresses. Selecting the right arrow advances to the next step.

visual.alt: Three consecutive LLM calls connected in sequence, with a gate placed after the first call in the chain diagram.
labels: Fail to pass then abort or retry

steps.title: What is chaining?
steps.body: Prompt chaining is a method of breaking down a task into sequential steps, where each LLM call uses the output of the previous call as its input. Instead of a single call handling everything, each call takes on a simpler, individual task.

steps.title: Step 1: Translation
steps.body: The first call only translates the product introduction text. It does not require simultaneous adherence to tone or terminology guidelines, so the focus is solely on the translation itself. The translated text becomes the input for the next call.

steps.title: Gate: Program Check
steps.body: Gate checks can be inserted between steps. For example, you can verify programmatically that all product names registered in the glossary appear without omission in the translation. If the check fails, the process halts or retries without proceeding to the next step. This allows you to detect deviations and verify that the flow remains on track.

steps.title: Step 2: Tone Calibration
steps.body: Only the translated text passing through the gate serves as input for the tone adjustment call. This call focuses exclusively on refining the tone without re-evaluating the accuracy of the translation. Clear roles are defined at each stage, making it easy to identify which stage caused a problem.

steps.title: Suitable tasks and transactions
steps.body: Chaining is ideal when the workflow is neatly divided into smaller, discrete subtasks. The core trade-off is accepting delay in exchange for improved accuracy. Each call becomes simpler, even though the overall number of calls increases and the total time taken grows.

steps.title: Another example of document delivery
steps.body: The document includes two examples. The first is a flow in which marketing copy is created and then translated into other languages, and the second is a flow in which the document outline is written first, and then the outline is checked to ensure it meets the required standards before writing the body content based on it. In both cases, the output of the earlier stage serves as the input for the subsequent stage.

labels: Branch A: Dedicated prompts and tools

tabs.label: Basic Concepts
tabs.body: Routing is a pattern that classifies inputs and forwards them to specialized follow-up actions. Different input types can have separate prompts and tools, enabling separation of concerns. Without routing, improvements tailored to one type of input could degrade the performance of other input types. Classification can be performed by an LLM, traditional classification models, or algorithms, but effectiveness is only achieved when inputs are classified accurately.

tabs.label: Customer Inquiry
tabs.body: An example of handling general inquiries, refund requests, and technical support queries separately. For refund requests, refund policy prompts and order lookup tools are provided; for technical support, troubleshooting procedures are established. Each category's prompt only needs to be tailored to its specific type of inquiry, resulting in simpler and more accurate handling.

tabs.label: Model Selection
tabs.body: A simple and common question is routed to a smaller, cost-efficient model, while a difficult and rare question is sent to a more powerful model. By not sending all requests to the largest model, we can reduce costs while maintaining performance. The document presents this as one approach to optimizing performance.

tabs.label: handoff
tabs.body: OpenAI's handoff refers to a method where a specialized agent receives the conversation from a particular branch, and can be viewed as a form of routing. The document assigns each expert a narrow role, provides a brief and specific explanation of the handoff, and recommends splitting only when the next branch truly requires different instructions, tools, or policies.

screens.outro: Now we will look at parallelization, where multiple individuals perform the same task simultaneously.

screens.title: Parallelization: Division and Voting
screens.lead: Compare how the same code review task differs when divided versus when voted on by alternately selecting two states.

visual.alt: A single input divided into three parallel calls, with results merged into code.

states.label: Partition
states.body: Splitting involves executing independent subtasks concurrently and then combining their results into code. In code reviews, security, performance, and readability are each assessed by separate calls happening simultaneously. An example with documentation is when one call handles user queries while another call filters out inappropriate requests through guardrails. This division generally results in better outcomes than a single call handling both tasks. In automated evaluation, each call assesses a different aspect as well. This approach provides the benefit of improved efficiency and allows each call to focus on a single perspective. However, the subtasks must be mutually independent.

states.label: Voting
states.body: Voting is a method of running the same task multiple times to obtain diverse outputs and increase confidence. For example, a configuration where multiple prompts independently review the same code change and indicate any issues they detect. When assessing content appropriateness, you can adjust the voting threshold to balance between false positives and false negatives. As the number of calls increases, costs rise but confidence in the results improves. Voting is suitable for high-cost, high-stakes judgments.

screens.outro: ADK's parallel and repetitive workflow documents also demonstrate the same principle. We will illustrate this with an example in the applicable screen.

screens.title: Explanation: Two design approaches for the document translation and quality review process
screens.lead: The instructor designs the same document translation task using chaining and parallel voting separately and compares them. Select the right arrow to proceed step by step.

steps.title: Task Definition
steps.body: Three types of reviews—accuracy, terminology, and tone—should be applied to the translated technical documentation. Design A uses chaining, while Design B uses parallel voting. The difference between the two designs lies in whether their review perspectives require each other's outcomes.

steps.title: Design A, Stage 1: Translation and Gate
steps.body: The first call translates the source text. Thereafter, the system checks in code whether any terms from the terminology database are missing from the translation. Since this is a mechanical check that does not require human judgment, it is processed directly via code, which is faster and cheaper. Translations that fail this check are not passed to the next stage.

steps.title: Design A, Stage 2: Tone Calibration
steps.body: Tone correction calls accept only the translated text that passes through the gate and refine it. Since the stages proceed sequentially, latency increases by the number of stages. However, when an issue occurs, it is immediately clear at which stage the problem arises, making error location easy to determine.

steps.title: Design B, Stage 1: Three perspectives simultaneously
steps.body: Submit the same translation text simultaneously to three independent reviews for accuracy, terminology, and style. Since these three perspectives do not require each other's results, there is no need to wait. Each review focuses on a single perspective. ADK's parallel workflow document also explains that such branching is effective when the branches are independent of each other.

steps.title: Design B, Stage 2: Voting Rules
steps.body: We establish a rule that if any of the three calls indicates an issue, the result is sent to human review. This is the code responsible for aggregating results. The ADK documentation explains that conversation records or state are not automatically shared between parallel branches. If sharing is required, it must be explicitly designed, and the order in which results are collected may not be fixed.

steps.title: Comparison of two designs
steps.body: Design A incurs delay that increases with the number of stages and makes it easier to locate error positions. Design B has shorter delays and more call overhead, and when viewpoints overlap, the same issues may be reported redundantly. There is no general rule as to which design is better—instead, the dependencies of the work determine the answer. In this case, since the three viewpoints are mutually independent, Design B is more appropriate. Conversely, since tone correction depends on the translation output, it involves sequential processing similar to Design A.

steps.title: Instructor's decision
steps.body: The determination criterion is whether the stages depend on each other. If one stage must complete before proceeding to the next, this is chaining; if independent perspectives or attempts are run simultaneously, this is parallelization. When input types diverge and require different handling, this is routing. In practice, a design that combines translation as a chain and review as parallel voting is naturally intuitive.

marks.span: Prompt chaining is used when the result from the previous step is available to proceed.
marks.note: The criterion for chaining is dependency between stages. By linking dependent stages sequentially and forcibly splitting independent stages, only delays are introduced.

marks.span: Two gates are used to prevent orbital drift.
marks.note: A gate is a point within the chain where a program checks the result. Failure is detected early and does not manifest until the end.

marks.span: If the input type varies, it is classified by routing and forwarded to specialized processing.
marks.note: Routing separates prompts and tools by input, preserving each other's performance. However, accuracy in classification is essential for effectiveness.

marks.span: Independent approaches or perspectives are parallelized and executed simultaneously.
marks.note: Partitioning provides speed and focus through independent subtasks, while voting obtains confidence through repeated execution of the same task. Parallel branching does not automatically share information.

marks.span: You should be able to explain in one sentence why that pattern is necessary.
marks.note: If the basis for choosing a pattern is not clear, there is a high likelihood of unnecessary complexity. You must be able to specify whether it is based on dependency, input type, or independence.

marks.span: The aspect of call count and latency
marks.note: All three patterns come with a cost. Chaining introduces latency, and parallelization increases call count and overhead. Division is only justified where there is a clear need to split.

glossary.def: This pattern divides the workflow into sequential steps, such that each LLM call processes the output of the previous call.
This is a point where the program checks the results during the chain execution to verify that the flow is correct.
A pattern that classifies input and sends it to a specialized follow-up task.
This is a parallelization approach that simultaneously executes independent sub-tasks and combines the results into code.
This is a parallelization approach that runs the same task multiple times to obtain diverse outputs and increase confidence.

misconceptions.myth: The more steps you divide it into, the better.
misconceptions.fact: Breaking down steps beyond where there is a clear need only increases delays. Divide only where there is a clear justification.

misconceptions.myth: Parallel calls automatically share information with each other.
misconceptions.fact: Parallel branching is independent execution, and conversation records or states are not automatically shared. Sharing must be implemented separately if required.

misconceptions.myth: Routing is not problematic even if the classification is incorrect.
misconceptions.fact: If classification is inaccurate, input is directed down the wrong path. When classification is accurate, the benefits of routing are realized.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Three patterns—dividing, branching, and executing simultaneously—are fundamental building blocks.
Chaining incurs latency to achieve accuracy and checks the intermediate steps via gates.
Routing maintains mutual performance by specialized handling according to input type.
Parallelization gains speed through partitioning and confidence through voting.

checks.q: What is the biggest reason for placing gates between steps in a prompt chain?
options: To reduce delays at each stage and improve overall speed
Reduce call volume to lower costs
Check via program whether the output of the previous stage meets the criteria to detect deviations early.
Combine multiple steps into a single prompt
checks.explain: A gate is a check that verifies, via code, whether the flow is on track within the chain. Chaining involves introducing delays and making transactions easier to process with each call, thereby achieving accuracy.

wrong.0: Chaining instead introduces delays proportional to the number of stages. Gates are not intended for speed improvement.
wrong.1: The gate adds inspection stages but does not reduce the number of calls.
wrong.3: The key point of chaining is dividing tasks; merging them leads back to the problem of a single prompt failing.

right: Run the same task multiple times to gain confidence in diverse outputs.

checks.explain: Chaining involves sequential dependency, routing involves classification followed by branching, partitioning enables concurrent execution of independent tasks, and voting increases confidence through repeated execution of the same task.

checks.q: We intend to apply accuracy, terminology, and style review to the same translated text. When the three perspectives do not require each other's outputs, what is the most appropriate structure?
options: A parallel voting mechanism that simultaneously executes three perspectives and forwards an issue for human review if any perspective identifies a problem
Chaining in the order of accuracy → term → tone
Classify the translation and select a single perspective for review routing
A structure where the central LLM dynamically generates and delegates inspection perspectives.
checks.explain: If perspectives are independently decoupled, both latency can be reduced and voting rules can be simplified to minimize locking. Chaining only makes sense when stages are mutually dependent.

wrong.1: When independent viewpoints are sequentially grouped, delay increases by the number of stages.
wrong.2: All three perspectives are necessary, so selecting only one results in missing the review.
wrong.3: Since the review perspective is predefined, there is no need to dynamically create subordinate tasks.
